blocks.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
blocks.passage:
Navigating a British hierarchy means reading the signals that organisation charts leave out. Two people with the same job title may sit very differently in the real pecking order — one may have the ear of the CEO, the other may be quietly on their way out. Nothing in the chart will tell you this. Observation will.

At the intermediate level, three signals matter most. Who speaks last in meetings — and whether everyone goes quieter when they start? Who gets the final email in a long thread, even if they wrote nothing? And who is invited to the small, undocumented conversations before the big decisions?

Once you know the answer to those three questions, you have understood the real hierarchy — and you can navigate it without stepping on anyone.

items.q: According to the text, what will the organisation chart NOT tell you?
options: Who really holds influence in the team
items.why: "Two people with the same job title may sit very differently in the real pecking order… Nothing in the chart will tell you this."

items.q: Which three signals does the author say matter most?
options: Who arrives first, who leaves last, and who talks most
Years of service, team size and budget
Who speaks last, who gets the final email, and who joins the informal conversations
Salary, office size and job title
items.why: O segundo parágrafo lista exatamente esses três sinais.

items.q: What is the reward for understanding the real hierarchy, according to the text?
options: A place on the org chart
Being able to navigate it without stepping on anyone
items.why: "you can navigate it without stepping on anyone."

items.q: The author would most likely DISAGREE with which statement?
options: Body language and timing can reveal authority.
The org chart is a reliable guide to who really decides.
Some influential people say very little in meetings.
items.why: Inferência: todo o texto argumenta que o organograma esconde a hierarquia real.

items.q: The line "the other may be quietly on their way out" suggests that…
options: someone with an impressive title may in fact be losing influence
quiet people are always the most powerful
job titles reliably reflect real standing
the person is leaving the building early
items.why: Inferência: mesmo cargo, situações opostas — um sobe, o outro está saindo silenciosamente.

blocks.instruction: Ouça James orientando um novo gestor. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
So, welcome to the team. Before you try to change anything, spend your first two weeks just watching. I mean it — say very little and observe a lot.

Here is the thing nobody puts in writing. On paper, Daniel and Priya are at exactly the same level. But watch what happens in the Monday meeting. When Priya finally speaks — and she always speaks last — the room goes quiet. People rewrite their slides after she comments. Daniel talks far more, but nobody changes anything because of it.

There's another tell. Look at the long email threads. Priya often writes nothing for days, and then the final message is hers, and that's the one everyone acts on. And before any real decision, there's usually a quiet coffee that never appears in anyone's calendar — she is always in it.

So my rule for you is simple: map the informal hierarchy before your second week is over. Find out who the room listens to, not who has the grander title. Get that wrong and you'll spend months pushing on doors that were never going to open.
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: What does James tell the new manager to do in the first two weeks?
options: Say very little and observe a lot
items.why: "say very little and observe a lot."

items.q: On paper, how do Daniel and Priya compare?
options: Daniel is more senior than Priya
They are at exactly the same level
items.why: "On paper, Daniel and Priya are at exactly the same level."

items.q: What sign shows Priya's real influence in meetings?
options: The room goes quiet and people rewrite their slides after she comments
She sits next to the CEO
items.why: "When Priya finally speaks… the room goes quiet. People rewrite their slides after she comments."

items.q: What does James imply about talking a lot in meetings?
options: It is the clearest sign of authority
It does not necessarily mean you have influence
It is discouraged in British companies
It always annoys the real decision-makers
items.why: Inferência: Daniel fala muito mais, mas nada muda por causa disso — volume não é poder.

items.q: What does James mean by "pushing on doors that were never going to open"?
options: Wasting effort on people who cannot actually decide
items.why: Inferência: se você mira quem tem o título mas não o poder, gasta meses sem resultado.

blocks.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "She has a modest title, but she sits near the top of the pecking order." Pecking order means…
options: the seating plan in the office
the informal ranking of power and influence
the order of the meeting agenda
items.why: Pecking order = ordem de hierarquia, o ranking informal de influência.

items.q: "If you want the budget approved, it helps to have the ear of the finance director." This means to…
options: have their trust and be listened to by them
sit next to them at lunch
items.why: To have the ear of = ter a confiança de alguém, ser ouvido por essa pessoa.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "The decision was made in an ___ conversation that never reached anyone's calendar."
items.why: Undocumented = não documentado; combina com a conversa que não aparece em lugar nenhum.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "When the senior partner started speaking, the room went ___ and everyone listened."
items.why: Quieter = mais silencioso; o sinal de que a pessoa realmente tem autoridade.

items.q: "Learning to navigate the hierarchy saved him months of frustration." To navigate means to…
options: find your way through it skilfully
items.why: To navigate = navegar/transitar, mover-se com habilidade dentro da estrutura.

blocks.instruction: Expressões e phrasal verbs comuns em ambientes corporativos. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "Try not to step on anyone as you settle into the team." To step on someone means to…
options: offend or undermine them, often without meaning to
items.why: To step on someone = pisar em alguém, passar por cima e ofender, muitas vezes sem querer.

items.q: "The director has to sign off on every hire." To sign off on means to…
items.why: Sign off on = aprovar formalmente, dar o aval final.

items.q: "Two team leads pushed back on the reorganisation." They…
items.why: Push back on = resistir, discordar — sem necessariamente rejeitar de vez.

items.q: "You need to read the room before you propose a big change." This means to…
options: sense the mood and reactions of the people present
items.why: Read the room = ler o ambiente, perceber o clima e as reações das pessoas.

items.q: "Once you know who really decides, everything else falls into place." This means it…
options: becomes clear and works out naturally
items.why: Fall into place = se encaixar, ficar claro e funcionar naturalmente.
